title: When the Body Fights
subtitle: Conflict is not a sign the church is failing. The refusal to face it is, and peace bought at any price is the most expensive thing a church can buy.

sections.title: A Church Without Conflict Is Not Healthy, It Is Suppressed
sections.body:
We assume a church in conflict is a church in trouble. Sometimes it is the opposite. A church with no visible conflict is often a church where the conflict has gone underground, where people swallow their disagreements and smile, where the peace on the surface is held in place by everyone agreeing not to say the true thing.

That is not health. That is suppression, and suppressed conflict does not disappear, it ferments, it leaks out sideways in gossip and triangulation and the slow poisoning of trust, until one day it erupts over something small and everyone is shocked, because they mistook silence for peace.

The New Testament churches fought. Paul and Barnabas had a disagreement so sharp they parted ways. The Jerusalem council convened because there was a genuine conflict that had to be settled. Euodia and Syntyche are named in Scripture for not getting along. Conflict is not the failure of the body. It is the body, made of real people with real differences, and the question is never whether you will have conflict but whether you will handle it like Christians or bury it like cowards.

sections.title: The Process Jesus Gave Us and We Ignore
sections.body:
Jesus gave the church a precise process for conflict in Matthew eighteen, and most churches ignore it completely. If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone. That is step one, and it is the step we skip every single time.

We do everything but that. We tell three other people. We pray about it loudly to a friend. We let it sit and curdle. We do anything except go directly to the person, alone, and speak the truth in love, which is the one thing Jesus actually commanded. The whole disaster of church conflict is built on the refusal of that first step, on a congregation that processes its hurts through gossip rather than confrontation.

Teach the process and then live it yourself, because the people will do what they see you do. Go directly. If that fails, take one or two others, witnesses, not allies recruited to your side. If that fails, bring it to the church. And at every stage the goal is stated plainly by Jesus, you have gained your brother. The aim is never to win, never to expose, never to punish. The aim is reconciliation, and a process aimed at anything else has already left the gospel behind no matter how many verses it cites.

sections.title: The Person Who Does Not Want Resolution
sections.body:
Most conflict is between people who, deep down, want it resolved. But there is a harder case, and every pastor who serves long enough meets it. The antagonist. The person whose aim is not reconciliation but power, not peace but control, who uses conflict as a weapon and has no intention of laying it down.

This person does not respond to Matthew eighteen the way a brother does, because Matthew eighteen assumes both parties want to be reconciled, and the antagonist does not. He wants to win, to divide, to gather a faction, to make the church bend to his will under threat of the damage he can do. And the pastor who treats the antagonist like a wounded brother, who keeps extending grace into a bottomless pit, will watch the antagonist consume the church while the pastor congratulates himself on his patience.

There comes a point, and Scripture names it, where you warn a divisive person once, then twice, and after that have nothing to do with them. Titus three. Paul tells the church to mark those who cause divisions and avoid them. This is not a failure of love. It is love for the ninety-nine, who are being damaged while the shepherd dotes on the wolf. Protecting the flock sometimes means standing between it and a person who will not be reconciled, and the pastor who cannot do that has confused niceness with shepherding.

sections.title: The Ruinous Price of Peace at Any Price
sections.body:
Jeremiah condemned the prophets who healed the wound of the people lightly, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace. That is the peace most churches choose. The false peace, the surface calm, the agreement not to address the thing, purchased by sacrificing the truth.

The pastor who will pay any price for peace ends up paying the highest price of all. He will not confront the sin, so the sin spreads. He will not address the conflict, so the conflict goes underground and rots. He will not stand against the antagonist, so the antagonist rules. And the church drifts toward a quiet death, all its real problems unspoken, all its members trained that nothing true is ever said out loud, and the pastor calls this unity when it is only fear wearing unity's face.

Real peace costs something different. It costs the hard conversation, the named sin, the conflict faced rather than buried. Jesus did not keep the peace, he made it, and making it sometimes meant overturning tables and calling things by their names. The peace he gives is not the absence of conflict. It is the presence of reconciliation on the far side of conflict honestly faced. The cheap peace avoids the cross. The real peace goes through it, and there is no other kind.

sections.title: I Have Chosen the False Peace
sections.body:
I have to end this one inside the indictment, because I have chosen the false peace more often than I want to admit. I have let a thing go that I should have confronted, because confronting it was hard and I was tired and I wanted the meeting to end. I have called my own conflict avoidance grace and patience and wisdom, and it was none of those things. It was fear.

And the fear always cost more than the conflict would have. The thing I would not address grew. The person I would not confront did more damage. The truth I would not speak festered in the silence I kept. Every time I bought the cheap peace, I paid for it later at a higher rate, and so did the church I was supposed to be protecting.

So I am not writing this as a man who has mastered conflict. I am writing it as a man who keeps relearning that the avoided confrontation is the most expensive thing in ministry, and that the courage to face the body's fights honestly is not the opposite of love but its hardest form.

The conflict you are avoiding right now is not going to disappear. It is going to wait, and grow, and cost you more the longer you leave it. Go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone. It is the bravest sentence Jesus ever asked of us, and we will do almost anything to avoid it.
